title: HTML style guide and maintainable markup
learningObjectives: Explain html style guide and maintainable markup and its role in modern HTML.
Select the correct elements, attributes, APIs, or browser behaviour for a practical use case.
Distinguish current practices from obsolete, limited, or legacy techniques.
Build and inspect a working example while considering accessibility and maintainability.
Diagnose common implementation errors and explain the trade-offs of the chosen approach.

understand.concept: An HTML style guide defines consistent conventions for document structure, indentation, casing, quoting, naming, comments, whitespace, and file organization. HTML element and attribute names are case-insensitive in text/html, but lowercase is the conventional readable form. Quote attribute values, use meaningful alt text, avoid unnecessary wrappers and obsolete elements, and keep nesting clear. Consistency matters more than a personal formatting preference; a team should document one convention and apply it through review or automated formatting.
understand.whyItMatters: Consistent markup makes code easier to review, debug, diff, and maintain across contributors. A style guide also reduces accidental accessibility and security omissions.
understand.analogy: A style guide is a shared set of road markings: people can travel different routes while still understanding the same signals.
understand.analogyLimit: A style guide is not a substitute for semantic correctness, browser validation, accessibility testing, or security review.

explain.narrative: Compare inconsistent markup with a normalized version. Identify which changes affect readability only and which changes improve actual semantics or accessibility.

examples.explanation: The element uses lowercase names, quoted attributes, a clear class name, and an explicit button type. The accessible name is useful because the visible text already says Save; in this example the aria-label is illustrative and may be redundant in a real interface.
The image has quoted attributes, meaningful alternative text, and intrinsic dimensions that help reserve layout space. The alt text should describe the image's purpose in context.
examples.expectedOutput: A team photo with reserved 640 by 360 layout dimensions.

practise.guidedTask: Reformat a deliberately inconsistent HTML page using one documented convention. Fix ambiguous class names, missing quotes, unclear nesting, and inappropriate empty alt text.
practise.independentTask: Write a one-page team HTML style guide and apply it to a small site. Review the diff to separate formatting-only changes from semantic corrections.
hints: Use lowercase element and attribute names for consistency.
Quote attribute values and use meaningful, consistent class names.
Do not add ARIA labels or roles when native HTML already provides the required semantics.

questions.prompt: Why use a shared HTML style guide?
options: To make markup consistent and easier to maintain
questions.answer: To make markup consistent and easier to maintain
questions.explanation: Shared conventions reduce review friction and improve readability.

questions.prompt: Which attribute style is recommended for readability?
questions.explanation: Quoting attribute values avoids ambiguity and is a strong consistent convention.

questions.prompt: What is the best class name?
questions.explanation: Purpose-oriented names remain meaningful when visual design changes.

questions.prompt: Does consistent indentation guarantee semantic correctness?
questions.explanation: Formatting helps readability but cannot replace correct element choice and validation.
